stops.name: Tintagel Castle, Cornwall
stops.campa: On the wind-scoured headland of Tintagel, where Uther Pendragon came to Igraine wearing Gorlois's stolen shape by Merlin's art, the infant Morgen is born, third and last daughter of Gorlois, Duke of Cornwall, and Igraine, before ever a crown touches Uther's brow. The sea below carves the rock into a narrow neck; the castle stands nearly an island already, half in this world and half not. No chronicle marks the day. She is the youngest of the three sisters, dark-haired, quick-eyed, and the tales that later call her half a fairy begin, the countryfolk say, on this very stone.

stops.name: The nunnery of Amesbury
stops.campa: Uther's decree sends the duke's orphaned daughters to be raised apart from Igraine's new husband's court, and Morgan is placed in a nunnery, the same house, tradition later insists, where a widowed Guinevere will end her own days. The sisters set her to her letters; she masters the seven liberal arts far past what the rule requires, and turns hardest to astronomy and to the healing virtues of herbs, working, the chroniclers say, wonderfully and without ceasing. It is here, before any sword is drawn for her brother Arthur, that the clerks first call her a great clerk of necromancy.
stops.quote: And the third sister Morgan le Fay was put to school in a nunnery, and there she learned so much that she was a great clerk of necromancy.
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book I, Chapter II (Caxton, 1485)

stops.name: Bedegraine forest (Sherwood)
stops.campa: Grown and restless at Arthur's young court, Morgan seeks out Merlin in the great forest of Bedegraine during one of his long absences and will not let him go until he has taught her more: the deeper arts of illusion, of shape and season, of binding and unbinding. He teaches her, the Prose Merlin says, working hard at it all the while she asks, more of necromancy than any woman of the realm will hold again. She takes the learning eagerly and outpaces her teacher's caution; what she means to do with it, Merlin does not yet ask, and will regret not asking.
stops.quote: the castle of Bedegraine, that was one of the castles that stand in the forest of Sherwood
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book I, Chapter XVII (Caxton, 1485)

stops.name: Caerleon-upon-Usk, the marriage to King Uriens
stops.campa: At Caerleon-upon-Usk, where Arthur holds his early court above the River Usk, Morgan is given in marriage to King Uriens of Gore, an alliance sealed like her sisters' to bind the kingdoms of Britain around her brother's throne. She is a queen still short of twenty. The marriage gives her a son, Yvain, who will grow into one of the finest knights of the Round Table and, in time, into the one man who dares raise a sword against his own mother when her arts turn murderous. For now the wedding feast is only a wedding feast, and no one reads the omen in it.

stops.name: Glastonbury Tor, Insula Pomorum
stops.campa: West across the Summer Country rises the green tor the Britons call Ynys Witrin, the Isle of Glass, and the poets call Insula Pomorum, the Island of Apples: a Fortunate Isle needing no plough, where fruit and grain come of themselves from the grass. Nine sisters rule it under a single gentle law, and Morgen is the eldest and most skilled of them, learned in every herb that cures a sick body, and mistress of an art stranger still: to change her shape and cleave the air on new wings, like Daedalus, and be seen at Brest, at Chartres, at Pavia, all in a single evening.
stops.quote: The island of apples which men call "The Fortunate Isle" gets its name from the fact that it produces all things of itself... Morgen is her name, and she has learned what useful properties all the herbs contain, so that she can cure sick bodies. She also knows an art by which to change her shape, and to cleave the air on new wings like Daedalus.
stops.quote_source: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Vita Merlini (c. 1150), lines on the Island of Apples

stops.name: Glastonbury Tor, the healing of Arthur
stops.campa: After the last battle at Camlann, they carry the wounded Arthur down to the water and set him in a ship steered by Barinthus, who alone among them knows the stars and the ways of the sea well enough to find the island. They come to Avalon, and Morgen receives them with fitting honour, lays the king on a golden bed in her own chamber, and uncovers the wound with her own hand. She looks at it long. At length she says health can be restored to him if he will stay with her a long while and use her healing art; rejoicing, they entrust him to her and sail home.
stops.quote: Thither after the battle of Camlan we took the wounded Arthur, guided by Barinthus to whom the waters and the stars of heaven were well known. With him steering the ship we arrived there with the prince, and Morgen received us with fitting honour, and in her chamber she placed the king on a golden bed and with her own hand she uncovered his honourable wound and gazed at it for a long time.
stops.quote_source: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Vita Merlini (c. 1150), Taliesin's account of Arthur's crossing

stops.name: Glastonbury Abbey, the exhumation of 1191
stops.campa: Seven centuries and more after Camlann by any reckoning, the monks of Glastonbury Abbey, their church newly burned and their coffers empty, dig sixteen feet down between two ancient stone pyramids in the graveyard and strike a hollowed oak trunk holding two skeletons, a tall man's and a woman's, a lock of golden hair crumbling to dust the instant the air touches it. Between the bodies lies a leaden cross, and on it, so Gerald of Wales records, the monks read aloud: here lies buried the renowned King Arthur, with Guinevere his second wife, in the Isle of Avalon. Morgen's isle has become a graveyard with a deed to it.
stops.quote: Hic iacet sepultus inclitus rex Arthurus cum Wenneveria uxore sua secunda in insula Avallonia (Here lies buried the renowned King Arthur with Guinevere his second wife, in the Isle of Avalon).
stops.quote_source: The leaden cross recorded by Gerald of Wales, De Principis Instructione (c. 1193)

stops.name: Camelot, the plaster of Morgan
stops.campa: Arthur's tents stand on a plain beside a lofty forest full of stags and hinds, and Erec rides in torn open by the wounds of his own long adventure. The king draws a deep sigh at the sight of them and has brought out the plaster his sister made and gave him, sovereign against any hurt in nerve or joint. It is the gentlest thing the romances will ever say of Morgan: not sorceress but physician, not rival but sister, her name spoken at court without fear, her craft sought before any other's. Chrétien writes her this way once, in passing, before the later tellers turn the healer's hands to other uses.
stops.quote: and has a plaster brought which Morgan, his sister, had made. This plaster, which Morgan had given to Arthur, was of such sovereign virtue that no wound, whether on nerve or joint, provided it were treated with the plaster once a day, could fail to be completely cured and healed within a week.
stops.quote_source: Chrétien de Troyes, Erec et Enide (c. 1170), tr. W. W. Comfort (1914)

stops.name: Camelot, the love of Guiomar and the rupture with Guinevere
stops.campa: Morgan takes as her lover Guiomar, a knight of the court and, in some tellings, lord of Avalon himself, nephew to Guinevere. For a season it is a hidden joy. Then the queen, learning of it, judges the match beneath her nephew's station and works to end it, and Guiomar, whether from duty or from cooling love, lets the affair die. Morgan does not forgive an ended love; she reads in it not sorrow but betrayal, and swears against Guinevere and every knight of the Round Table a hatred that will outlast the reign itself. She leaves court that season to find Merlin again, and this time she does not come back the same.

stops.name: The land of Gore, the attempt on King Uriens
stops.campa: Believing her brother dead at Accolon's hands, Morgan sees King Uriens asleep and sends a maid of her counsel for his sword. The maid brings it with quaking hands, but first wakes Uwaine and tells him what his mother means to do. Morgan pulls the blade and stands over the bed, judging where to strike best, and as she lifts it her son leaps and catches her by the hand. She begs him: she was tempted with a devil, she will never do so again, let him save her worship and not discover her. Uwaine forgives her on that covenant, and keeps it.
stops.quote: Ah, said Sir Uwaine, men saith that Merlin was begotten of a devil, but I may say an earthly devil bare me.
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book IV, Chapter XIII (Caxton, 1485)

stops.name: Camelot, the poisoned mantle
stops.campa: A damsel comes from Morgan bearing the richest mantle ever seen in that court, set as full of precious stones as one might stand by another, with word that the king should take this gift of his sister and name any amends he pleases. It pleases Arthur much, and he says little. Then the Damosel of the Lake asks him in privity to let it come on no man until he has commanded the bringer to put it on herself. He does. The damsel falls down dead and burns to coals before the whole hall. Arthur turns on Uriens, names his sister a traitor, and banishes her son Uwaine.
stops.quote: And so the king made it to be put upon her, and forthwithal she fell down dead, and never more spake word after and burnt to coals.
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book IV, Chapter XVI (Caxton, 1485)

stops.name: Le Miroir aux Fées, Tréhorenteuc
stops.campa: West of Camelot, deep in the forest the Bretons will one day call Brocéliande, a still pool called the Miroir aux Fées lies at the mouth of a narrow valley, and the country people say seven fairy sisters once lived in its water and can still be seen there by anyone who looks long enough and truly. It is here that Morgan, newly broken by Guiomar, first sets down her grief and her power together, and the valley beyond the mirror, until now an ordinary green cleft in the woods, waits to become the place her name will never leave again.
